newsitem.title: ITALY: Food summit ends with pledge to world's hungry.
newsitem.headline: Food summit ends with pledge to world's hungry.

text.p: Pledging relief for the starving millions, world leaders end a summit on Sunday that has promised real action to tackle human misery in the 21st century.

The U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome, which has heard almost a week of speeches, has already adopted an "action plan" to halve the number of hungry people in the world from the current 840 million within 20 years.

It is expected to be the last for some time of the global summits that bloomed after the end of the Cold War, tackling everything from the environment to women's rights and poverty in conferences from Copenhagen to Beijing.
Like other U.N. meetings before it, the Rome summit has agreed a declaration but seen sharp differences between rich and poor nations.

Wealthy countries like the United States and its European allies put their faith in free trade, while many of the world's developing nations want more aid and sympathy from countries where hunger is not a daily struggle for most people.
The meeting has been overshadowed by the crisis in eastern Zaire, with the spectacle of thousands of starving refugees serving as a stark reminder of the problems.
Aid agencies, women's groups and other non-governmental organisations have criticised the summit declaration as bland and want a more radical approach.

They will issue their own declaration on Sunday. But they won support from veteran Cuban leader Fidel Castro, who brought life to an often lacklustre meeting by denouncing it on Saturday as inadequate and a fig leaf for the evils of capitalism.

In a firebrand speech, the 70-year-old communist denounced "capitalism, neoliberalism, the laws of a wild market, the external debt, underdevelopment and the unequal terms of reference that are killing so many people in the world".
"The rich do not know hunger," he said, to loud applause from leaders of developing nations.
While in Rome, Castro is to meet Pope John Paul for the first time, bringing together two of the leading figures of the 20th century. The meeting is at the Vatican on Tuesday.

The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) had promised that more than 100 world leaders would attend the meeting. In the end, only 86 turned up -- less than half the total membership of the United Nations.
Because of the resultant shortage of speakers, the summit was due to end earlier than planned on Sunday.

The summit declaration, approved earlier this week, is not legally binding but lays out suggested policies which governments say they will follow. It says everyone has the right to food and to be free from hunger and promises urgent international action to tackle the problem.
